standard.title: National identity debates
standard.description: different experiences of, perspectives on and debates about Australia's national identity and citizenship, including the perspectives of First Nations Australians as owners of their respective nations, and of different migrant groups
standard.prior_knowledge: Students understand how Australia's pluralist multi-faith society draws on diverse cultural origins (AC9HC7K04), the values supporting social cohesion (AC9HC7K05), and from K05 in this year level, how culture and religion shape citizenship expressions. The gap this descriptor fills is the explicitly contested dimension of national identity — not just that Australia is diverse, but that there are genuine, ongoing debates about what it means to be Australian, who belongs, and whose perspectives are centred or marginalised.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students analyse different experiences of, perspectives on and debates about Australia's national identity and citizenship, including the perspectives of First Nations Australians as owners of their respective nations and of different migrant groups.

nodes.label: Meaning of national identity and citizenship
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain what is meant by 'national identity', what it means to be an Australian citizen, and why national identity matters in a globalised world.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain what 'national identity' means and identify two elements that contribute to a sense of Australian national identity.
nodes.typical_width: Examine the meaning of 'national identity' — the shared values, symbols, stories and sense of belonging that define membership in a national community — and explain what it means to be an Australian citizen formally and culturally. Discuss why national identity remains significant in a globalised world.
wider: Investigate how 'Australian identity' has been defined differently at different historical moments — comparing representations from Federation, post-WWII immigration and contemporary multicultural Australia
Examine the tension between national identity and global or transnational identity for Australians with strong cultural or diasporic ties to other countries
Investigate how definitions of national identity shape citizenship policies — including the citizenship test and the oath of allegiance — and what values those definitions embed
nodes.hinge_reason: The concept of national identity — and the distinction between formal and cultural citizenship — is the lens through which all subsequent debate in this descriptor is conducted. If students do not have a working understanding of what national identity is and why it is contested, the debates about First Nations perspectives and migrant experiences cannot be engaged with meaningfully.

response_modes.reason: Students often conflate national identity with citizenship law. Invest in the conceptual distinction — national identity is cultural, contested and dynamic; citizenship is a legal status. Both matter and they interact but they are not the same thing.

success_criteria: Can explain what national identity means, distinguishing it from legal citizenship
Can identify at least two elements that contribute to a sense of Australian national identity

nodes.label: Different representations of Australian identity
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can analyse different representations of Australian identity — historical and current — examining how they reflect particular perspectives and whose experiences they include or exclude.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe one historical and one current representation of Australian identity and identify whose perspective each reflects.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse different representations of Australian identity historically and currently — including representations in national symbols, media, official narratives and popular culture — examining what values and experiences they foreground, whose perspectives they reflect and whose they marginalise or exclude.
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australian perspectives on national identity challenge or complicate mainstream representations of 'being Australian'

Examine how multicultural Australia is represented (and sometimes misrepresented) in national identity narratives — comparing official multicultural policy discourse with lived experiences of migrants
Analyse a specific national symbol (the flag, the anthem, Anzac Day) as a site of contestation about Australian identity, examining different perspectives on its meaning and appropriateness

response_modes.reason: Representations of national identity are numerous and varied. Widening across historical and contemporary examples, and across different symbolic contexts, prevents students from treating one representation as definitive.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Analysing representations of national identity is analytically rich because students must identify perspective and evaluate inclusion/exclusion — skills that transfer to media literacy and critical citizenship. Width across multiple representational contexts builds this analytical capability.
success_criteria: Can describe at least one representation of Australian identity and identify whose perspective it primarily reflects
Can identify at least one group or perspective that is marginalised or excluded by a given representation of Australian identity

nodes.label: Factors shaping national identity debates
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate the factors shaping debates about Australian identity, including place, immigration and standard of living.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain how one factor (place, immigration or standard of living) shapes debates about Australian national identity with a specific example.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate the key factors that shape ongoing debates about Australian identity — including how place (geography, connection to land, urban vs regional), immigration (changing composition of the population, multiculturalism, migration policy) and standard of living (economic circumstances, class and inequality) each influence how people understand and contest Australian identity.
wider: Investigate how population growth, changing immigration patterns and demographic change are reshaping debates about Australian identity in specific communities or regions
Examine how the relationship between place and identity operates differently for First Nations Australians (for whom Country is constitutive of identity) compared with settler Australians

Investigate how economic inequality shapes different Australians' experience of national identity — examining whether 'the Australian dream' is equally accessible across different socioeconomic groups

response_modes.reason: The three named factors (place, immigration, standard of living) are genuinely distinct and each opens different debates. Widening across all three prevents students from treating national identity debates as reducible to a single driver.

success_criteria: Can explain how at least two of the named factors (place, immigration, standard of living) shape debates about Australian identity
Can give a specific example illustrating one of those factors in action

nodes.label: Migrant experiences and citizenship choices
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain why some migrants choose to become Australian citizens while others do not, and what this reveals about the meaning of citizenship.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two reasons why a migrant might choose to become an Australian citizen and at least one reason why some might choose not to.
nodes.typical_width: Explore the reasons why migrants elect to become Australian citizens — including legal rights, sense of belonging, political participation, security of residency — and why others choose not to, including retention of existing citizenship, lack of dual citizenship arrangements, cost or difficulty of the process, or attachment to original national identity.
wider: Investigate how Australia's dual citizenship policy affects the decisions of migrants from countries that do not allow dual citizenship
Examine the experiences of refugees and humanitarian entrants in navigating citizenship — how their pathway to citizenship differs and what it represents for them
Investigate how the Australian citizenship test has changed over time and what debates about its content reveal about contested definitions of Australian identity

response_modes.reason: Migrants' citizenship choices are not monolithic — they vary by origin country, legal status, cultural attachment and life circumstances. Widening across different migrant contexts prevents oversimplified generalisations.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Exploring why migrants do and do not choose citizenship brings abstract concepts (belonging, identity, rights) into lived experience. Width across different migrant contexts — economic migrants, refugees, dual-citizenship-seeking migrants — builds genuine empathetic and analytical understanding.
success_criteria: Can identify at least two reasons why a migrant might choose to become an Australian citizen
Can identify at least one reason why some migrants choose not to become citizens

nodes.label: National symbols and identity: citizenship test and anthem
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can analyse how national symbols such as the citizenship test and the national anthem contribute to and reflect debates about Australian national identity.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain how either the citizenship test or the national anthem reflects a particular vision of Australian national identity.
nodes.typical_width: Examine the citizenship test — the types of questions asked and what vision of Australian identity they embed — and discuss how the national anthem contributes to national identity, examining whose stories and perspectives it does and does not include. Connect both to broader debates about Australian identity.
wider: Analyse debates about changing the Australian national anthem — examining different perspectives on whether the anthem adequately reflects contemporary Australia, including First Nations perspectives
Investigate how citizenship tests in different countries vary and what values different nations embed in their citizenship requirements

Examine how First Nations Australians relate to national symbols such as the Australian flag and anthem — and what debates about changing these symbols reveal about unresolved questions of national identity

response_modes.reason: National symbols integrate all the threads of this descriptor — national identity, representation, migrant experiences, First Nations perspectives. Use this node to draw together the different dimensions of identity debate covered throughout K06.

success_criteria: Can explain how either the citizenship test or the national anthem reflects a particular view of Australian identity
Can identify at least one perspective (e.g. First Nations, migrant) that raises questions about whether those symbols adequately represent all Australians
